title: Overview of modernizing a .NET monolith on AWS
content:
A .NET FRAMEWORK APP HAS RUN “JUST FINE” FOR 10 YEARS, SO WHY MODERNIZE IT? CHOOSING THE RIGHT PATH TO MOVE A .NET MONOLITH TO AWS I also posted this article in the AWS Study Group (FCAJ) Facebook group: view the post. The group is private, so only members can open the link.
Many companies still run ASP.NET applications written on .NET Framework, on Windows Server and Microsoft SQL Server. The application still works, but every release means the whole team is on call, newcomers need weeks to understand the code, the old framework is hard to patch and hard to hire for, the system is hard to scale, and Windows and SQL Server licenses have to be paid every year.
Today I want to share an overview of how to modernize a .NET monolith on AWS, which I learned from the AWS Architecture Blog, together with the recent AWS changes that I double-checked while writing. The thing I noticed most: there is no single sequence of steps for every application. Some phases are mandatory, some are prerequisites for other phases, and some should only be done when really needed.
Note before reading: the original article (published 19/05/2022) uses Microservice Extractor for .NET, App2Container and Porting Assistant for .NET. Since 07/11/2025, AWS has stopped onboarding new customers to these tools (existing customers can still use them to finish their projects) and introduced AWS Transform for .NET (an AI-agent service that converts .NET Framework code to cross-platform .NET) as the replacement. In this post I list both the tools from the original article and the current ones.
Starting architecture:
Web tier: user interface (ASP.NET MVC or Web Forms). Application tier: business logic on .NET Framework, running on Windows Server + IIS. Data tier: Microsoft SQL Server. Phase 0: Assess (mandatory)
Inventory NuGet packages, native libraries and the parts that only run on Windows: Web Forms, WCF, COM/COM+, Windows Registry, Windows Authentication, IIS-specific configuration. Inventory stored procedures, triggers, SQL Server Agent jobs and the degree of T-SQL dependency. Analyze the business logic and how tightly the parts of the code are coupled. Measure the baseline: current performance, total cost of ownership (TCO), RTO/RPO requirements. Tools: the repository assessment feature of AWS Transform for .NET combined with a manual inventory. Output: an assessment report, a list of risks, and the decision on which phases to continue with. Phase 1: Stabilize and replatform
Set up CI/CD (build, scan, push the image to Amazon ECR, deploy, rollback) and manage infrastructure with IaC (CloudFormation, CDK or Terraform). Containerize the monolith. The original article uses App2Container, which no longer accepts new customers, so new projects write a Dockerfile. Amazon ECR is only where images are stored; containers run on Amazon ECS. If it is still .NET Framework, run Windows containers on Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate (ECS Fargate for short; supports Windows Server 2019/2022, x86_64 only, and does not support some features such as EFS, FSx, gMSA, Fargate Spot) or on ECS on EC2 when you need those features or control over the host. The database can be moved to AWS without changing the engine yet (for example Amazon RDS for SQL Server), using AWS DMS (full load + CDC) or SQL Server native backup/restore. Turn on logging, monitoring, backup and basic security from this phase. Note: containerization only gives a consistent deployment environment; it does not solve technical debt. The application still depends on Windows, IIS and SQL Server. Phase 2: Modernize .NET
Port from .NET Framework to .NET 10 (LTS release, published 11/2025, supported until 11/2028; .NET 8 ends support on 10/11/2026). The original article uses Porting Assistant for .NET. For new projects, AWS recommends AWS Transform for .NET, a new service that replaces the older group of tools rather than a renamed Porting Assistant. Transform still has limits on project types, and its results need human review and testing. Web Forms has no equivalent in ASP.NET Core. AWS Transform can port a Web Forms UI to Blazor Server (.aspx/.ascx become .razor, Web.config becomes appsettings.json), but this is automation-assisted UI porting, not an equivalent conversion: Web Forms uses the page lifecycle, PostBack and ViewState, while Blazor uses components. Third-party controls, .svc and .ashx files and Web Site projects still have to be handled manually, and UI behavior must be retested. Moving to .NET 10 does not mean it will run on Linux. Only drop Windows Server after replacing Windows-only APIs and running integration tests on Linux (including authentication, file system, timezone, encoding and certificates). AWS Graviton (ARM64) only applies to Linux containers (Windows containers do not run on Graviton; Fargate ARM64 needs platform version 1.4.0 or later). Graviton is worth considering to reduce cost, but not every native library has an ARM64 build. You need to build the image for the right architecture and benchmark against x86_64 first. The figure “Fargate Graviton2 is up to 20% cheaper” comes from the 2022 original article; for my own workload I need to recalculate with the AWS Pricing Calculator. Where to run: ECS Fargate for always-on applications, AWS Lambda for short jobs or event handling (in this post Lambda is not a public API). Phase 3: Modernize the database (optional)
This is the riskiest phase. You can keep SQL Server (on RDS) if the conversion is not worth the effort. If you convert, there are two directions:
Direction A, move fully to PostgreSQL: the target is RDS for PostgreSQL or Aurora PostgreSQL. This is not one automatic operation but 4 separate steps: Convert the schema: AWS DMS Schema Conversion (the AWS documentation recommends it instead of AWS SCT, which is now called the legacy version) converts the schema and database objects, with a list of action items to fix by hand. This step does not move data. Migrate the data: the data migration task of AWS DMS (full load, then CDC). Fix and test the application: adjust queries and drivers and re-check the business logic. Cutover: reconcile the data, check replication lag, pause writes (write freeze) and have a rollback plan. AWS Transform (since 12/2025) can also convert SQL Server to Aurora PostgreSQL (the only target of this workflow): schema, T-SQL stored procedures to PL/pgSQL, and ADO.NET/Entity Framework code. This workflow only supports .NET 6 and later applications and does not support .NET Framework 4.x, so Phase 2 must be finished first. Direction B, Babelfish for Aurora PostgreSQL: a compatibility layer that lets Aurora understand T-SQL and the SQL Server protocol, so less code needs to change. Babelfish is not SQL Server running on PostgreSQL and does not support all of T-SQL; you need to run Babelfish Compass and test with a real workload first. Which direction? With many stored procedures, heavy T-SQL dependency and code that is hard to change, consider Babelfish. With little T-SQL, code you can change and a wish to use standard PostgreSQL long term, choose Direction A. Being able to convert the syntax does not mean it runs correctly. Common differences: data types, collation and case sensitivity, identity and sequences, temporary tables, locking and transaction behavior, cross-database queries, SQL Server Agent jobs, and execution plans. DMS CDC only syncs data; the actual downtime also depends on the volume of changes, long transactions and replication lag. You need to reconcile data, benchmark performance, rehearse the cutover and have a rollback plan. Phase 4: Re-architect (optional)
Modernization does not mean microservices. Splitting services brings network latency, distributed transactions, eventual consistency, harder debugging and higher operating cost. A modular monolith (still deployed as one unit but divided into clear business modules) fits when the team is small and the business logic is not too complex. Microservices fit when clear bounded contexts exist, independent scaling or release is needed, and there is enough capability to operate a distributed system. Without a strong enough reason, stop at a modular monolith. If you split: use DDD to define business boundaries and split gradually in the strangler fig style. The original article uses Microservice Extractor for .NET; this tool has no direct replacement, because AWS Transform for .NET focuses on converting code to cross-platform .NET rather than splitting an application into services. Designing the boundaries is still the team’s job. Also split data ownership: each service has its own schema and database user with permissions only on its own schema; other services get data through APIs or events. You also need a communication mechanism (for example SQS, EventBridge), retries, dead-letter queues and tracing. Phase 3 and Phase 4 can be swapped depending on how tightly the application is coupled to the database. A possible target architecture (after Phase 2; the database depends on Phase 3):
Users reach the app through an Application Load Balancer (HTTPS, certificate from AWS Certificate Manager) in a public subnet. The security group of the ECS tasks only accepts traffic from the ALB; add AWS WAF if the threat model requires it. The .NET 10 application runs on ECS Fargate in a private subnet. This can still be a monolith, a modular monolith or microservices, depending on Phase 4. Tasks pull images from Amazon ECR through the ECR VPC endpoints (api, dkr) and the S3 endpoint (S3 holds the image layers). These endpoints only serve image pulls. If you use CloudWatch Logs, Secrets Manager or KMS without NAT, you need the matching endpoints as well. Calling external APIs still needs a NAT Gateway or an outbound proxy. AWS Lambda runs short jobs triggered by Amazon EventBridge (event or schedule). EventBridge is not in the VPC; it calls Lambda through invoke permission. Lambda only needs to be attached to the VPC when it must reach private resources such as the database; then a security group must allow the connection to the database. If Lambda runs with high concurrency, use RDS Proxy or limit concurrency so it does not open too many connections. Attaching to a VPC also does not give Internet access by itself; you need NAT to call out. The database sits in a private subnet: Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL if you do Phase 3 (turn on Babelfish if you choose Direction B); if you skip Phase 3, keep Amazon RDS for SQL Server from Phase 1. The diagram shows the case where Phase 3 is done. AWS DMS runs in the VPC and connects to the on-premises SQL Server over Site-to-Site VPN or Direct Connect. The DMS target is RDS for SQL Server (Phase 1) or Aurora PostgreSQL (Phase 3). You need to check routes, firewalls and security groups to both the source and the target, and grant permission to read the transaction log for CDC. The simplified diagram only draws 1 AZ. In production: the ALB and ECS service span at least 2 AZs (with health checks, autoscaling and a deployment strategy), the database has a replica in another AZ for failover, and there are backups that have been tested by restoring. This is an overview diagram, not a production reference architecture. My summary table:
Phase Mandatory? Output / completion criteria Main risk 0. Assess Mandatory Assessment report, risk list, chosen phases Skipping it puts the whole project at risk 1. Stabilize + replatform Recommended Running on AWS with CI/CD, rollback, monitoring Low; Windows containers are heavy, technical debt not reduced 2. Modernize .NET When you need to drop Windows or the old framework Running .NET 10, passing integration tests on Linux (and ARM64 if Graviton is chosen) Medium; Web Forms, WCF, Windows-only libraries 3. Database Optional Reconciled data matches, performance meets baseline, rollback rehearsed High; behavioral differences between SQL Server and PostgreSQL 4. Re-architect Optional Services with clear boundaries and data owners High; complexity of a distributed system About cost: moving to Linux can remove the Windows OS cost of the workload, but how much you save depends on how it runs. With Windows containers on Fargate, the Windows Server license is already included in the Fargate price (charged extra per vCPU), so I do not buy a separate license; with ECS on EC2 it depends on the instance’s license model. The SQL Server cost only disappears when you really change the engine to PostgreSQL, and then Aurora/RDS, conversion, testing and operating costs appear. You should compare TCO before and after (compute, database, storage, network, monitoring, license, conversion effort) instead of looking only at licenses.
Out of scope for this post (each point is enough for its own post): detailed design of communication between services, a full testing strategy (characterization tests, regression, load tests), detailed cutover and rollback plans, and security and monitoring (WAF, Secrets Manager, KMS, CloudWatch, X-Ray, CloudTrail).
What I learned:
Modernization is not “tear it down and rebuild”, and it does not require moving to microservices. Many systems only need a replatform, or .NET 10 + a modular monolith, to solve most of their problems. Moving to a newer framework does not mean runtime compatibility: .NET 10 does not remove Windows dependencies by itself, and PostgreSQL is not automatically equivalent to SQL Server. Each phase needs measurable completion criteria instead of only expected benefits. The biggest lesson from writing this post: an old blog post must be re-checked against current documentation. The original was written in 2022; since then many tools have stopped accepting new customers, and the recommended .NET version and the schema conversion tool have both changed. Conclusion:
Instead of a fixed 4-step sequence, start with assessment, stabilize the system on AWS, and only then modernize .NET, the database and the architecture when there is a clear reason. AWS Transform for .NET is an option worth evaluating for the code conversion part, after checking its supported scope, compatibility and cost. The diagram in this post is an overview picture for learning, not a complete production architecture.
Personal perspective: this post is my synthesis from several sources (the original AWS Architecture Blog article, AWS and Microsoft documentation) and the still-limited view of someone who is learning, so it surely has gaps. I would really appreciate feedback from everyone, especially those who have done .NET modernization in practice.

title: Proposal
content:
RoomLedger A Serverless AWS Platform for Boarding-House Management with Tamper-Proof Photo Records and AI Meter Reading 1. Executive Summary In large Vietnamese cities, disputes between boarding-house landlords and tenants usually come down to two things: the deposit at move-out (was the room damaged?) and the monthly electricity and water bill (what did the meter really show?). Both sides often have only verbal agreements or a few photos sent over chat. RoomLedger is a serverless web application on AWS, deployed in ap-southeast-2 (Sydney), with three roles: administrator, landlord and tenant, sized for 31–51 users (one boarding house with 30–50 rooms). It stands out with two features: move-in photo records that are locked with Amazon S3 Object Lock once both sides confirm, and Amazon Bedrock (Claude Haiku 4.5) reading electricity and water meter photos to produce the monthly bill. Paper contracts are scanned, confirmed by the tenant and stored.
2. Problem Statement What’s the Problem? Move-in records are often missing, or they are just a few scattered photos on each person’s phone, so at move-out the two sides have no shared evidence. Photos can be claimed to be taken later, taken in another room, or edited. Each month the landlord reads the meters alone, and tenants who never see the meter tend to doubt the numbers. Existing Vietnamese boarding-house apps (LOZIDO, Quản Lý Phòng Trọ Việt Nam) handle invoices, contracts and payment reminders well, but have no photo-based handover record and no AI. Foreign apps (Witnessed, PropCheckAI, DepositCam) record handover photos, but they do not manage boarding houses and do not require confirmation from both sides.
The Solution RoomLedger puts locked, two-party-confirmed photo records, AI meter reading and a move-out review into one flow together with contracts, monthly invoices and deposit settlement. The Angular web app is served from Amazon S3 through Amazon CloudFront, users sign in with Amazon Cognito, and API calls go through Amazon API Gateway protected by AWS WAF to AWS Lambda (.NET 8) running in private subnets of an Amazon VPC. Data is stored in Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL (Multi-AZ). The API Lambda writes business events to an S3 outbox bucket, and S3 forwards them to Amazon EventBridge. Photos are uploaded directly from the browser to Amazon S3 with a presigned URL and a SHA-256 checksum, flow through Amazon EventBridge and Amazon SQS to the photo-processing Lambda, and are copied to an evidence bucket with Object Lock when the record is locked. For meter photos, AWS Step Functions calls Amazon Bedrock to read the value; the landlord confirms it and the app issues the invoice. At move-out the landlord compares move-in and move-out photos of the same area side by side and enters deductions; the tenant accepts or disputes each item. AI does not compare photos.
Benefits and Return on Investment Landlord and tenant share one move-in record that both have confirmed and nobody can change, including the administrator. Every meter reading has a meter photo behind it, and the paper contract has a scan confirmed by both sides. Benefits are measured on demo data: time to record utilities for 10 rooms (manual versus photo + AI) and AI meter-reading accuracy. Production costs about 80.62 USD/month, roughly 1.6–2.7 USD per room per month. Almost all of it is fixed hourly cost (RDS Multi-AZ, the Cognito Interface endpoint, WAF), so growing from 31 to 51 users barely changes the bill. There is no NAT Gateway or load balancer, S3 traffic uses a free Gateway endpoint, and AI is only used for meter reading with a low-cost model. The app gives both sides a shared basis for negotiation; the project does not claim the record has legal standing in court.
3. Solution Architecture RoomLedger uses a serverless architecture on AWS with a single production environment in ap-southeast-2 (Sydney). The API, photo-processing, post-confirmation and migrate Lambdas run in private subnets across two Availability Zones with no NAT Gateway and no load balancer. They connect to RDS over TLS with RDS IAM authentication and reach S3 through a Gateway endpoint. Instead of calling EventBridge directly, the API Lambda writes events to an S3 outbox bucket through the Gateway endpoint, and the outbox bucket sends them to EventBridge, so no EventBridge Interface endpoint is needed. The only Interface endpoint is Cognito (one per AZ), used by the post-confirmation Lambda to add users to groups. The AI and notification Lambdas run outside the VPC, so no Bedrock or SES endpoint is needed. All infrastructure is written in AWS CDK (C#) and deployed from GitHub to AWS CloudFormation through OIDC.
AWS Services Used Amazon CloudFront: Serves the Angular web app from S3 and forwards API requests to API Gateway. AWS WAF: Regional Web ACL on API Gateway that blocks abnormal traffic and rate-limits requests, including requests that bypass CloudFront. Amazon Cognito: Two user pools, one for landlords and tenants, one for administrators with mandatory MFA. Amazon API Gateway (REST API): API entry point with a Cognito authorizer. AWS Lambda (.NET 8): API, photo processing, post-confirmation and migrate inside the VPC; AI meter reading and notifications outside the VPC. Amazon EventBridge: Receives events from the S3 outbox and incoming buckets and routes them (new photo, record locked, meter reading, settlement, notification). Amazon SQS: Photo queue in front of the photo-processing Lambda plus a dead-letter queue, absorbing bursts without losing events. AWS Step Functions: Orchestrates meter reading: calls the AI Lambda, retries on failure, then passes the result to the photo-processing Lambda, which saves it to RDS for the landlord to approve. Amazon Bedrock (Claude Haiku 4.5): Reads electricity and water meter values from photos; the only place AI is used. Amazon S3 and S3 Glacier Deep Archive: Four buckets: incoming (deleted after 7 days), outbox (events, deleted after 7 days), derived (previews, PDFs) and evidence (Object Lock, encrypted with KMS); old evidence moves to Glacier Deep Archive. Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL: db.t4g.micro Multi-AZ, 20 GB gp2, encrypted, SSL enforced, IAM authentication. Amazon VPC: Private subnets in two AZs, Gateway endpoint for S3, Interface endpoint for Cognito in each AZ; no NAT Gateway. AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store: Model ID and prompt for the AI Lambda, changeable without redeploying. AWS IAM, AWS KMS and AWS Secrets Manager: Least-privilege role per Lambda; customer managed key for the evidence bucket; Secrets Manager only holds the RDS master password created by CDK, while Lambdas sign in with RDS IAM authentication. Amazon GuardDuty and AWS CloudTrail: Threat detection and audit trail. Amazon SES: Sends invite links, invoices and notifications. Amazon CloudWatch, Amazon SNS and AWS Budgets: Logs, dashboard, alarms emailed through SNS, and cost alerts. AWS CloudFormation (AWS CDK) and GitHub Actions (OIDC): Infrastructure as code, deployed without stored AWS keys. Component Design Web Application: Angular UI for three roles; computes the SHA-256 of the original file before uploading to S3. Contracts and Move-in Records: Contract scans and condition photos are locked once both sides confirm; nobody can edit or delete them. Utilities and Invoices: AI reads meter values from photos and flags uncertain readings or readings lower than last month; the landlord confirms and sends the invoice. Move-out: Move-in and move-out photos of the same area are shown side by side; the landlord enters deductions, the tenant accepts or disputes each item, then the app settles the deposit and produces a termination PDF. Access Control and Audit Log: Each landlord sees only their own data and each tenant only their room; every action and every denied access is logged. Events: the API Lambda writes events to the S3 outbox (outbox pattern); EventBridge routes them to SQS, Step Functions and the notification Lambda. Data: EF Core code-first on PostgreSQL; idempotent migrations run through the migrate Lambda only at deploy time. 4. Technical Implementation Implementation Phases
The project is built in four phases during the five implementation weeks:
Foundation: CDK infrastructure (two-AZ VPC and endpoints, RDS, four S3 buckets, two Cognito user pools, API), CI/CD with OIDC, Angular skeleton for three roles, data model and access control. (Week 8) Contracts, Move-in and Invoices: properties, rooms, invite links, contract scans, photo records and locking, AI meter reading and monthly invoices. (Weeks 9–10) Move-out: side-by-side photo review, deductions, disputes, deposit settlement, termination PDF. (Week 11) Finalization: security tests, AI meter-reading evaluation, demo and workshop. (Week 12) Technical Requirements
Frontend: Angular, Angular Material and WebCrypto; desktop UI for landlords and administrators, mobile UI for tenants. Backend: .NET 8 on Lambda: ASP.NET Core and EF Core (Npgsql) for the API; separate Lambdas for photo processing (Magick.NET for HEIC to JPEG, EXIF), Bedrock calls through the AWS SDK for .NET, and PDF generation with QuestPDF. Infrastructure: AWS CDK (C#), GitHub Actions with OIDC, one team AWS account in ap-southeast-2 with AWS Budgets alerts. Dataset: move-in and move-out photos of two real rooms, about 30 meter photos (mechanical, digital, water) with known values, and a few sample contract scans. 5. Timeline & Milestones Project Timeline
Weeks 1–5: Learn AWS (core services, serverless, security, IaC) and complete the workshops. Weeks 6–7: Learn while shaping the idea: research the problem, compare existing products, design the architecture and UI, write the proposal. Weeks 8–12: Build the project: Week 8: Foundation; original photos uploaded to S3 with checksum verification, all three roles can sign in. Weeks 9–10: Contracts, move-in and invoices work end to end. Week 11: Move-out and deposit settlement. Week 12: Security tests, demo and final report. 6. Budget Estimation The estimate was made with the AWS Pricing Calculator for Asia Pacific (Sydney), production running 24/7 across 2 AZs, 31–51 active users per month, Before Discount rates. Removing the EventBridge and Secrets Manager Interface endpoints (replaced by the S3 outbox and RDS IAM authentication) lowered the estimate from 99.60 to 80.62 USD/month, a saving of about 19 USD/month.
Infrastructure Costs AWS Services: Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL: $42.75/month (db.t4g.micro Multi-AZ 730 hours $37.23, 20 GB gp2 Multi-AZ storage $5.52) Amazon VPC: $18.98/month (Cognito Interface endpoint in 2 AZs, 1,460 hours; 0.1 GB processed) AWS WAF: $10.01/month (1 Web ACL $5.00, 5 rules $5.00, 20,000 requests) Amazon CloudWatch: $4.64/month (1 dashboard $3.00, 15 alarms $1.50, about 0.2 GB of logs) Amazon Bedrock (Claude Haiku 4.5): $1.49/month (input tokens $1.22, output tokens $0.27) AWS KMS: $1.00/month (1 customer managed key, 400 requests) AWS Secrets Manager: $0.80/month (2 secrets including the RDS master password, 200 API requests) Amazon SQS: $0.26/month (650,000 requests, mostly Lambda long-polling the photo queue) Amazon S3: $0.16/month (about 8 GB, evidence bucket on Intelligent-Tiering) Amazon CloudFront: $0.14/month (1 GB data transfer, 20,000 HTTPS requests) Amazon GuardDuty: $0.14/month (6,000 events, 0.1 GB of logs) Data Transfer: $0.14/month (1.2 GB out to the internet) AWS Lambda (ARM), API Gateway, SES, CloudTrail, EventBridge, SNS: $0.10/month (11,000 API requests, 100 emails) Amazon Cognito: $0.00/month (31–51 MAU within the free tier) Total: $80.62/month, $967.44/12 months
7. Risk Assessment Risk Matrix Tenant uploads old photos or photos of another room at move-in: High impact, medium probability. AI misreads a meter: Medium impact, medium probability. Access-control bug between landlords: High impact, low probability. iPhone HEIC photos cannot be sent to Bedrock directly: Medium impact, high probability. AI model fails, is throttled or returns a wrong format: Medium impact, medium probability. Contract scan differs from the tenant’s paper copy: High impact, low probability. Mitigation Strategies Old or wrong photos: warn on EXIF capture date; the record is valid only after both sides confirm. Meter readings: always confirmed by a person; uncertain readings or readings lower than last month are flagged. Access control: checked per record in the API; covered by access-control tests. HEIC: the photo-processing Lambda converts to JPEG for analysis and keeps the original. AI model: JSON output against a schema, a fallback model, and model switching through Parameter Store without redeploying. Contract scan: the tenant must confirm before locking and can press “Not correct”. Contingency Plans If Bedrock is unstable for the demo, meter reading runs on a fixed demo photo set and the landlord enters values manually when AI cannot read them. If costs rise unexpectedly, AWS Budgets alerts the team to review and limit Bedrock calls. 8. Expected Outcomes Technical Improvements: Move-in photo records locked with S3 Object Lock and confirmed by both sides, with security tests for evidence locking, access control and WAF. AI meter reading replaces manual recording, with a report on accuracy and time saved.
Long-term Value A reusable pattern for tamper-proof photo evidence on AWS (checksum upload, Object Lock, two-party confirmation, audit log), fully defined in AWS CDK. Future work: bank transfer reconciliation, photo incident reports during the tenancy, Zalo notifications and a mobile app.

title: Securing a legacy .NET application on AWS
content:
IS THE CONNECTION STRING STILL IN WEB.CONFIG? SECURING A LEGACY .NET APPLICATION AFTER MOVING IT TO AWS I also posted this article in the AWS Study Group (FCAJ) Facebook group: view the post. The group is private, so only members can open the link.
In Blog 1, I shared a path for modernizing a .NET monolith on AWS: assess, replatform, move to .NET 10, and only then think about the database and the architecture. But there is one question I did not answer: once the application runs in containers, how does security change?
On-premises, many old .NET applications are secured in a “the firewall is enough” way: the database password sits in Web.config, the application runs as an IIS app pool account, users sign in with Windows Authentication, and everything trusts everything else because it is all inside the internal network. On AWS, these assumptions no longer hold.
Today I want to share what I learned about securing the target architecture from Blog 1, split into 4 pillars: secrets management, IAM roles, authentication, and network and data security.
Context: the application after Phase 2 of Blog 1
A .NET 10 application runs as a Linux container on Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate (ECS Fargate for short) in a private subnet. Users reach it through a domain name on Amazon Route 53, then Amazon CloudFront, and only then the Application Load Balancer (ALB) in a public subnet. The database is Amazon RDS for SQL Server (or Aurora PostgreSQL if Phase 3 is done). The original application uses on-premises Active Directory for sign-in and for the database connection. The application is still a monolith running as one ECS service. Throughout this post, the database connection has two options: (A) SQL Authentication with credentials in Secrets Manager (simpler), or (B) domainless gMSA with Active Directory (when the AD integration must be kept). Pillar 1: Secrets Management
Web.config or appsettings.json often holds a connection string with the user and password in plain text, and the file often gets committed to the repository. AWS Prescriptive Guidance also points this out as a common risk for .NET applications. You do not need to move the whole connection string to AWS Secrets Manager. The non-sensitive parts (server, database name, timeout) can stay in config; only the credentials (user, password, API key) go into Secrets Manager. Sensitive configuration that does not need rotation can use Parameter Store (SecureString). There are two ways for a container to get a secret on ECS: Declare it in the task definition (secrets + valueFrom): ECS fetches the value and puts it into an environment variable when the task starts. Simple, no code change, but after the secret changes you have to start a new task to get the new value. The application reads it through the AWS SDK, with the AWSSDK.SecretsManager.Caching library so it does not call the API on every request. This way can pick up the new value after rotation, but the application has to handle it: a sensible cache refresh time, opening new connections with the new credential (connections already open in the pool still use the old session), and retrying on temporary authentication errors during rotation. Rotation is not on by default; it has to be configured for the database and the authentication method: RDS can let Secrets Manager manage the master user password and rotate it every 7 days by default. But the application should not use the master user. The application’s own user is rotated by a rotation Lambda function: Secrets Manager calls the Lambda on a schedule, the Lambda creates a new password, updates the user in the database, and then updates the new version of the secret in Secrets Manager. Secrets Manager does not change the database by itself. This Lambda runs inside the VPC so it can reach the database; choose the single user or alternating users strategy (switching between two users so connections do not drop when the password changes). If the secret comes in through the task definition, you have to start new tasks after rotation (force new deployment); if it is only read once at startup, connections will fail. You should also monitor for failed rotations. If the database connection uses Windows Authentication (see pillar 3), there is no database password to rotate; instead there is the secret of the AD account used to get the gMSA. Pillar 2: Identity & Access
On ECS there are two roles that are very easy to confuse:
Task Execution Role: used by the ECS/Fargate agent, not by the application code. This role pulls the image from Amazon ECR, writes logs to CloudWatch Logs, and fetches the secrets declared in the task definition. The container cannot use this role’s permissions. Task Role: used by the application code when it calls AWS APIs at runtime, for example reading a file on S3, sending a message to SQS, or reading a secret through the SDK. Least privilege applies to each role separately: the execution role can only read that service’s own secrets and repository; the task role only has the actions the application really needs, scoped to specific ARNs instead of *. For a monolith running as one ECS service, you only need one minimal task role for that workload. When it is split into several services (Phase 4 of Blog 1), each service gets its own task role, so if one service is compromised the blast radius is as small as possible. Compared with on-premises, where every application on the server shares the IIS app pool account, permissions are now tied to each workload. Do not put access keys in the container. ECS gives the task role temporary credentials and rotates them automatically. Pillar 3: Authentication
There are two separate problems: users signing in to the application, and the application authenticating to other systems (database, file share).
Application users: if the application is moved to OIDC/SAML sign-in, Amazon Cognito (user pool) is one option, not a required component. The ALB can authenticate through Cognito or OIDC before the request reaches the application, and Cognito can federate with AD FS or Microsoft Entra ID through SAML so employees keep using their company accounts. However, Cognito does not directly replace Windows Authentication: it does not issue Kerberos tickets and does not work with gMSA or NTFS permissions. Also, the ALB only authenticates at the HTTP layer and passes the user information (claims) down; the application still has to read the claims, map roles/groups and do its own business authorization. Workloads that need Active Directory: AWS Managed Microsoft AD (AWS Directory Service) fits better when the application needs Kerberos, gMSA, or Windows Authentication to SQL Server. RDS for SQL Server supports Windows Authentication with AWS Managed Microsoft AD, or joining a self-managed AD directly (including on-premises AD if there is network connectivity, supported since 07/2023). Another way to keep on-premises identities is to use AWS Managed Microsoft AD with a forest trust to the on-premises AD. AD Connector is not a supported option for this feature. This post uses AWS Managed Microsoft AD as the example, but it is not the only option. gMSA in containers: a gMSA (group Managed Service Account) gives the application an AD identity without embedding a static password. Windows containers on ECS Fargate do not support gMSA; if you need it, use ECS on EC2 (as Blog 1 mentioned). Since 03/2024, ECS Fargate supports domainless gMSA for Linux containers through the built-in Credentials Fetcher (the task does not join the domain). This is one option to keep the AD integration after moving to .NET 10 on Linux, not something you just switch on. The main requirements: Fargate platform version 1.4.0 or later; each task can only use one Active Directory. The CredSpec file is stored on S3; the AD account used to get the gMSA (username, password, domainName) is stored in Secrets Manager. The task execution role can read exactly that secret and that CredSpec object (plus KMS permissions if the secret is encrypted with a customer-managed key). The VPC can resolve the AD domain name (DHCP options pointing to the AD DNS) and the task can reach the domain controllers. The connection string uses the SQL Server FQDN that matches the registered SPN, not an IP address; DNS, the Kerberos realm and time sync must be correct. On Linux, do not count on a fallback to NTLM like on Windows. You need real testing with the .NET version, Microsoft.Data.SqlClient and the RDS SQL Server version you use. Two different identities: Cognito authenticates users; gMSA (or a SQL credential) authenticates the workload when it connects to the database. A gMSA is not the identity of each user signed in to the website; passing the end user’s identity down to the database is a separate Kerberos delegation problem. Pillar 4: Network & Data Security
The edge layer: Amazon CloudFront sits in front of the ALB and receives HTTPS requests at the edge location closest to the user. An AWS WAF web ACL is attached to the CloudFront distribution, so requests are filtered at the edge before they reach the VPC: managed rules (SQL injection, XSS, bad IPs) and a rate-based rule against request flooding. CloudFront and Route 53 are protected by AWS Shield Standard against common network-layer DDoS attacks by default, at no extra cost. WAF only protects at the HTTP request layer; it does not replace authentication, IAM or security groups. Only let CloudFront reach the ALB: otherwise users can still call the ALB directly and skip WAF. Following the CloudFront documentation, CloudFront adds a secret custom header to requests it sends to the origin, the ALB listener only forwards requests that carry that header (others get a 403), and the ALB security group only allows the AWS-managed prefix list for CloudFront. Another option is CloudFront VPC origins, which lets you place an internal ALB in a private subnet. Security groups are chained, referencing each other instead of opening IP ranges: ALB SG: only accepts 443 from the CloudFront prefix list. ECS task SG: only accepts the application port from the ALB SG. Database SG: only accepts 1433 (SQL Server) from the ECS task SG. If you choose option B (gMSA): the task also needs a path to AWS Managed Microsoft AD (DNS, Kerberos, LDAP as listed in the Directory Service docs), or to on-premises AD over VPN/Direct Connect. Tasks in the private subnet get secrets from Secrets Manager and the CredSpec from S3 through VPC endpoints or NAT. Encryption in transit: HTTPS from users to CloudFront and from CloudFront to the ALB, with certificates from AWS Certificate Manager (ACM); the CloudFront certificate must be created in us-east-1, and the ALB certificate in the ALB’s Region; the connection to SQL Server uses TLS (Encrypt=True in the connection string, and it can be enforced with the rds.force_ssl parameter). The Linux container must trust the RDS CA certificate (add the RDS CA bundle to the image) for the TLS connection to work. Encryption at rest: RDS encrypts the database, backups and snapshots with a KMS key; Secrets Manager encrypts secrets with a KMS key (AWS KMS manages the keys, it does not store the data). Choose a customer-managed key when you need to control the key policy, key rotation or audit key usage. Note: RDS encryption must be turned on when the instance is created; for an existing unencrypted instance you have to copy a snapshot with encryption and restore it. Alongside the 4 pillars: logging & monitoring
Security without logs means that when something goes wrong, you cannot tell what happened. These are the log sources and monitoring services I think should be turned on from the start:
AWS CloudTrail records every AWS API call: who called what, when and from where. Create a trail that delivers logs to S3 so they are kept long-term for audits. CloudWatch Logs receives application logs from containers through the awslogs log driver. Set a retention period for each log group, and never write secrets or connection strings to logs. Request-layer logs: WAF logs go to CloudWatch Logs (the log group name must start with aws-waf-logs-), S3 or Firehose; ALB access logs and CloudFront logs go to S3. VPC Flow Logs record metadata about network traffic in the VPC. Amazon GuardDuty detects threats by analyzing CloudTrail, VPC flow logs and DNS logs; its Runtime Monitoring feature also supports ECS on Fargate to watch behavior inside containers. AWS Security Hub collects findings from GuardDuty, Inspector and other services in one place, and checks configuration against best-practice standards. The architecture after applying the 4 pillars:
(1) Users open the application domain (for example app.example.com); Amazon Route 53 resolves it through an alias record that points to the CloudFront distribution. (2) Users send HTTPS requests to the nearest CloudFront edge location. (3) The WAF web ACL attached to CloudFront filters them, and Shield Standard protects against network-layer DDoS. (4) CloudFront forwards only allowed requests to the ALB over HTTPS, with the custom header; the ALB only accepts traffic from CloudFront. If the application uses OIDC/SAML, the ALB sends users to Cognito to sign in. (5) The ALB forwards requests to the ECS Fargate task in the private subnet (its SG only accepts traffic from the ALB). (6) The task connects to the database as described below. When the task starts, the execution role pulls the image from ECR, fetches secrets from Secrets Manager and writes logs to CloudWatch Logs. At runtime, the application code uses the task role to call other AWS APIs (S3, SQS…). With option B, the execution role also reads the CredSpec from S3 and the AD account from Secrets Manager so Credentials Fetcher can get the gMSA Kerberos ticket from the domain controller. The task connects to RDS for SQL Server over TLS in one of two ways: (A) a user/password from Secrets Manager, or (B) Windows Authentication through domainless gMSA with AWS Managed Microsoft AD (the task needs a path to AD). RDS and Secrets Manager encrypt data with KMS keys. If a user/password is used and rotation is configured, Secrets Manager calls the rotation Lambda on a schedule to change the password in the database and update the secret. AWS Managed Microsoft AD is a shared directory service in the VPC, placed in its own subnets rather than belonging to the database. By default it runs two domain controllers in two AZs; production needs to plan for the availability of the directory. The whole system is logged and monitored: CloudTrail writes API calls to S3, application and WAF logs go to CloudWatch Logs, ALB and CloudFront logs go to S3; GuardDuty analyzes these sources to detect anomalies and sends findings to Security Hub. My summary table (before and after):
Pillar On-premises (before) On AWS (after) 1. Secrets Plain-text password in Web.config Credentials in Secrets Manager, rotated if configured 2. Access IIS app pool account shared on the server Execution role + minimal task role per workload 3a. User sign-in Windows Integrated Authentication OIDC/SAML federation (for example Cognito + the company IdP), if the application is converted 3b. Application to database AD service account SQL credential from Secrets Manager (A) or domainless gMSA (B), depending on compatibility needs 4. Network and data Trust the internal network, perimeter firewall CloudFront + WAF + Shield at the edge, ALB only reachable from CloudFront, chained security groups, TLS, KMS Logging and monitoring Logs scattered across servers CloudTrail, CloudWatch Logs, WAF/ALB/CloudFront logs, GuardDuty, Security Hub Out of scope for this post: software supply chain security (image vulnerability scanning and image signing in the pipeline), managing the team’s access to AWS accounts (IAM Identity Center), and service-to-service security after splitting into microservices.
What I learned:
Moving to AWS does not make an application more secure by itself. I have to actively replace the old assumptions (“same network means trusted”) with clear authentication and authorization at every layer. Many services are easy to see as “replacements” for each other, but each one solves its own problem: Cognito authenticates users while gMSA authenticates the workload, WAF does not replace security groups, and the execution role is not the task role. “Having rotation” only means something when the application can read the new secret. A security feature only works when both the application and the infrastructure support it. Conclusion:
For a legacy .NET application, security on AWS starts with taking credentials out of configuration files, granting least privilege through IAM roles, and choosing the right authentication for users and for the workload, and only then adding the network and encryption layers. These four pillars should be considered from Phase 1 of the modernization path, instead of after the system is already in production.
Personal perspective: this post is my synthesis from several sources (AWS Prescriptive Guidance, the AWS Containers Blog, the AWS Security Blog and AWS documentation) and the still-limited view of someone who is learning, so it surely has gaps. I would really appreciate feedback from everyone, especially those who have secured .NET applications on AWS in practice.

title: Cost optimization for a .NET application on AWS
content:
ALREADY IN CONTAINERS, NO MORE WINDOWS LICENSES, SO WHY IS THE AWS BILL STILL HIGH? COST OPTIMIZATION FOR A .NET APPLICATION AFTER MODERNIZATION I also posted this article in the AWS Study Group (FCAJ) Facebook group: view the post. The group is private, so only members can open the link.
In Blog 1, I shared a path for moving a .NET monolith to AWS, and Blog 2 covered how to secure that architecture. The remaining question is the one every manager asks after a few months in production: why didn’t the bill go down as expected?
Moving to .NET 10 on Linux does remove the Windows OS cost of the workload. But the AWS bill has many other items: compute running On-Demand 24/7, an Enterprise database running even for dev, a NAT gateway charging for every GB, logs kept forever. None of these go down unless you actively optimize them.
Today I want to share what I learned about cost optimization for the target architecture from Blog 1, split into 4 groups: cost visibility, compute, database, and network and logs. At the end there is a real example from OrderServ, a .NET platform that cut its compute cost by up to 64%.
Context: the application after Phase 2 of Blog 1 (and secured as in Blog 2)
A .NET 10 application runs as a Linux container on Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate (ECS Fargate for short) in a private subnet, behind Amazon Route 53, Amazon CloudFront with AWS WAF, and an Application Load Balancer (ALB), as drawn in Blog 2. The database is Amazon RDS for SQL Server (or Aurora PostgreSQL if Phase 3 is done). Secrets are in Secrets Manager, logs go to CloudWatch Logs, and tasks reach the Internet through a NAT gateway. There are at least two environments: production and dev/test. Group 1: See the cost before optimizing it (Cost visibility)
You cannot optimize what you cannot measure. This step should be done from day one on AWS.
Tag resources (for example Project, Environment, Owner) and activate them as cost allocation tags in Billing. For ECS, turn on enableECSManagedTags and propagateTags so the tags are added to every task. This lets you separate production cost from dev/test cost. AWS Cost Explorer shows cost by service, by tag, and by ECS cluster and service, with 13 months of history and a 3-month forecast. AWS Budgets sets a budget for each environment and sends alerts when actual or forecasted cost goes over the threshold. Cost Anomaly Detection uses machine learning to detect unusual cost increases (for example, someone forgot to turn off a test environment) and sends alerts by email or SNS. Cost Optimization Hub collects savings recommendations (rightsizing, Savings Plans, Reserved Instances) in one place, including ECS tasks on Fargate and RDS. Before changing the architecture, use the AWS Pricing Calculator to compare options instead of guessing. Group 2: Compute (ECS Fargate)
Right-size first, commit later. Task definitions are often given CPU/memory “to be safe” during migration and never changed. AWS Compute Optimizer gives CPU and memory recommendations for ECS services on Fargate based on real usage. Reduce the size first and only then buy Savings Plans, otherwise you commit to paying for resources you are wasting. Graviton (ARM64): on Fargate, Linux/ARM vCPU and memory are about 20% cheaper than x86. .NET 10 runs well on linux-arm64, but you need to build a multi-architecture image and check that native libraries (drivers, image or PDF processing libraries) have ARM64 builds. Fargate Spot: up to 70% off Fargate On-Demand, but tasks can be reclaimed with a 2-minute warning (SIGTERM and an EventBridge event). Fargate Spot is Linux only and does not support Windows. It fits dev/test environments, batch jobs, or part of the tasks of a service that can tolerate interruption; for production, use a capacity provider strategy with a base on FARGATE so a minimum number of tasks always runs On-Demand. Compute Savings Plans: commit to an hourly spend for 1 or 3 years and get up to 50% off Fargate. The plan applies flexibly to EC2, Fargate and Lambda, so it still works if you later change how compute runs. Turn off unused environments: dev/test ECS services can scale to 0 tasks outside working hours (for example with scheduled scaling). Many teams skip this step even though it is the simplest saving. Still running Windows containers? Fargate Windows adds an OS license fee per vCPU, with a 5-minute minimum charge per task (1 minute on Linux), and Savings Plans do not discount this license fee. This is the economic reason to do Phase 2 (moving to .NET on Linux) in Blog 1. Group 3: Database (RDS for SQL Server)
For a legacy .NET application, the database is usually the biggest cost, mainly because the SQL Server license is included in the RDS price (License Included).
Pick the right edition: RDS for SQL Server offers Express, Web, Standard and Enterprise. Many systems move to Enterprise because on-premises used Enterprise, while Standard might be enough. Check whether the application really uses Enterprise-only features. Web edition is cheaper but, under Microsoft’s license terms, may only be used for public web workloads, so it is not an option for every internal application. Dev/test environments: since 12/2025, RDS for SQL Server supports Developer Edition for non-production environments. It uses a bring your own media model (you upload the installation media to S3) and has no SQL Server license fee. Do not run dev/test on Enterprise License Included. Dev/test environments usually do not need Multi-AZ either. Optimize CPU: the SQL Server license is charged per vCPU. For 2xlarge and larger instances, RDS can reduce the number of vCPUs (turn off hyperthreading or reduce cores) to reduce the license part when the workload does not need that much CPU. Reserved Instances: a database that runs steadily 24/7 should use RDS Reserved Instances for 1 or 3 years. Note that an RI cannot change region, edition, instance class or term after purchase, and it does not cover storage, so right-size first. Rightsizing the database: Compute Optimizer has recommendations for RDS and Aurora, but only for MySQL and PostgreSQL; it does not support RDS for SQL Server. For SQL Server, you have to review CPU, memory and IOPS metrics yourself in CloudWatch and Performance Insights. Phase 3 (moving to Aurora PostgreSQL): this is the only way to remove the SQL Server license completely, but in exchange there are conversion, testing and operating costs. Once on Aurora, choose Aurora I/O-Optimized when I/O makes up more than 25% of your total Aurora cost. Group 4: Network & logging
These are small items, but they often surprise people on the bill.
A NAT gateway is charged per hour and per GB of data processed (about 0.045 USD/hour and 0.045 USD/GB in US East). If tasks in the private subnet pull images and call AWS APIs through NAT, every deployment costs money. A gateway VPC endpoint for S3 (and DynamoDB) is free, so turn it on so S3 traffic does not go through NAT. Interface endpoints (ECR, Secrets Manager, CloudWatch Logs) avoid NAT too, but they are charged per hour in each AZ and per GB; compare against your real traffic before creating many endpoints. Public IPv4: since 02/2024, every public IPv4 address is charged 0.005 USD/hour, whether it is in use or not. Fargate tasks do not need a public IP if they are already in a private subnet. CloudFront in front of the ALB: besides the security role described in Blog 2, CloudFront also affects cost. AWS waives the data transfer charge between CloudFront and AWS origins such as the ALB, cached static content no longer hits the ECS tasks, and WAF at the edge drops junk requests before they use compute. Log retention: CloudWatch Logs log groups default to never expire. Set a suitable retention (for example 30 or 90 days), and export logs that must be kept longer to S3. The Essentials log class (formerly Infrequent Access) has a lower ingestion price than the Standard class, but it lacks some features such as Live Tail, metric filters and subscription filters, and the log class cannot be changed after the log group is created. It fits application logs that are mostly used for lookups during incidents; logs used for alarms or metric filters should stay in Standard. The architecture after applying the 4 groups:
All resources have Environment and Project tags; Cost Explorer, Budgets and Cost Anomaly Detection track cost per environment. The production ECS service runs right-sized tasks on Graviton (ARM64); the minimum number of tasks runs on Fargate On-Demand covered by Compute Savings Plans, and extra tasks can use Fargate Spot. Dev/test scales to 0 outside working hours. Production RDS for SQL Server uses the right edition, Optimize CPU and a Reserved Instance; dev/test uses Developer Edition in Single-AZ. S3 traffic goes through the free gateway endpoint; the NAT gateway is only used for traffic that really needs the Internet. Log groups have a clear retention, and rarely accessed logs use the Essentials class. A real example: OrderServ cut compute cost by up to 64%
According to a post on the AWS Architecture Blog (05/11/2026), OrderServ is a food-ordering platform for many restaurant brands, with 21 microservices written in .NET. Before, each brand had its own ECS cluster on Fargate, adding a new brand took days of infrastructure work, and during traffic spikes new Fargate tasks needed 5-7 minutes to become ready.
They moved to one shared ECS cluster for all brands, isolating data with a shared .NET library (a tenancy library), IAM session tags per tenant and ElastiCache RBAC. Compute moved from Fargate to an EC2 Auto Scaling group running Bottlerocket with a warm pool: instances are pre-initialized in a stopped state, cost only EBS (about 3 USD/month per instance), and start in 30-60 seconds. The discount comes from Compute Savings Plans. For 21 services in ap-south-1: Fargate On-Demand is about 1,568 USD/month; EC2 + warm pool + a 1-year Savings Plan is about 832 USD/month (~47% less); with a 3-year Savings Plan it is about 568 USD/month (~64% less). Passkey sign-in reduces SMS costs, and adding a new brand is now a configuration change that takes minutes. What I find worth noting: for a small monolith like the one in Blog 1, Fargate is still a simple and sensible choice. But when the workload is large, steady and spiky, EC2 + warm pool + Savings Plans can be both cheaper and faster to scale, in exchange for the team managing EC2 capacity itself.
My summary table (before and after):
Group Common after migration After optimization 1. Cost visibility One shared bill, no idea which environment costs money Cost allocation tags, Cost Explorer, Budgets, Cost Anomaly Detection 2. Compute Task size “to be safe”, x86, On-Demand 24/7 even for dev/test Right-size, Graviton, Savings Plans, Fargate Spot for interruption-tolerant parts, dev/test off outside working hours 3. Database Enterprise License Included for every environment Right edition, Developer Edition for dev/test, Optimize CPU, Reserved Instances 4. Network and logs All traffic through NAT, logs kept forever S3 gateway endpoint, no unneeded public IPs, retention, Essentials log class Out of scope for this post: optimizing data transfer between regions and to the Internet (CloudFront), storage and backup costs (S3 lifecycle, snapshots), a FinOps model for the whole organization, and the cost of the security tools from Blog 2 (WAF, GuardDuty).
What I learned:
Moving to AWS does not make the bill cheaper by itself. Removing the Windows license is only one part; items like the database, NAT and logs are where money usually “leaks”. Order matters: measure, right-size, then commit (Savings Plans, Reserved Instances). Committing before right-sizing locks in the waste for 1-3 years. Many cost decisions are architecture decisions. Fargate or EC2, SQL Server or PostgreSQL, NAT or VPC endpoints all have trade-offs between cost, operational effort and complexity. Conclusion:
For a .NET application after modernization, cost optimization starts with seeing where the money goes, right-sizing compute and the database, choosing the right way to buy (Savings Plans, Reserved Instances, Spot), and then cleaning up the small items in networking and logs. Like security in Blog 2, cost should be considered from the start of the modernization path, instead of waiting for the first monthly bill to be surprised.
Personal perspective: this post is my synthesis from several sources (the AWS Architecture Blog, AWS documentation and pricing pages, and First Cloud Journey workshops) and the still-limited view of someone who is learning, so it surely has gaps. Prices in this post are for reference only (mostly US East) and can differ by region and over time. I would really appreciate feedback from everyone, especially those who have optimized costs for .NET workloads on AWS.

title: Event 3
content:
Summary Report: “Fireside Chat with Dr. Werner Vogels” Event Objectives Meet and talk with Dr. Werner Vogels, CTO of Amazon Hear his view on the future of Cloud and AI Learn from Amazon’s experience building and running systems at global scale Speakers Dr. Werner Vogels – Chief Technology Officer & Vice President, Amazon My Nguyen – Sr. Prototyping Architect, AWS Vietnam Key Highlights The story behind Dynamo Amazon once had its system down for a whole day during the shopping season because its relational database was overloaded → millions of dollars lost Looking back, most of the data only needed simple key-value lookups, and very little really needed a relational database So Amazon built its own key-value store, the ancestor of DynamoDB How Amazon runs its systems Don’t look at the average, look at P99.9 to see what the slowest users are going through “Everything fails all the time” → design the system to keep running when a data center fails GameDays: deliberately shut down real data centers to test whether the system can fail over on its own “Renaissance Developer” A developer in the AI era needs to: stay curious and keep learning, think in systems, own the code they ship, go deep in one area while understanding the others, and communicate well with the team and customers AI is just a tool AI makes prototyping much faster, but the code it writes still has to be checked by a human Grace Hopper said: “The most dangerous phrase is: ‘We’ve always done it this way.’” Key Takeaways Choose technology based on what the system really needs, not out of habit Always be prepared for the system to fail Developers are still needed with AI around, as long as they keep learning and take ownership of their work Applying to Work Review and test AI-written code carefully before using it (security, edge cases, …) Look at how the data is actually used before choosing a database for a project Event Experience Hearing Amazon’s CTO speak in person was a really memorable experience. Some highlights:
Real stories from someone who was there Instead of theory, Werner told real incidents and decisions from Amazon, which made it easy to understand why AWS services are designed the way they are The part about developers in the AI era made me worry less and showed me which skills I need to work on Event Photos

Cost optimization for a .NET application on AWS Blog 3 completes the series with cost optimization for the .NET application after modernization, in 4 groups: cost visibility (tags, Cost Explorer, Budgets, Cost Anomaly Detection), compute (right-sizing, Graviton, Savings Plans, Fargate Spot), database (SQL Server edition, Developer Edition for dev/test, Reserved Instances), and network and logs (NAT gateway, VPC endpoints, log retention).
